body:
What is an inscription?

An inscription is writing engraved on a durable surface such as stone, metal or pottery. Ancient Indian rulers used inscriptions to communicate instructions, record achievements, commemorate public works and preserve important events. The study of inscriptions is called epigraphy.

Unlike a manuscript, which is written on material such as palm leaves or paper, an inscription is engraved directly onto a surface. An inscription may therefore preserve the words of a ruler or an official long after the kingdom that produced it has disappeared.

The inscriptions studied in this lesson belong mainly to 2 categories: royal edicts and prashastis.

  • Royal edict: An order, instruction or public message issued by a ruler. Ashoka's rock edicts are important examples.
  • Prashasti: A composition praising a ruler's achievements, victories or qualities. The Prayaga Prashasti of Samudragupta and the Aihole inscription praising Pulakeshin II are important examples.

A prashasti may contain useful historical facts, but its purpose is also to praise its patron. Descriptions of victories and personal qualities should therefore be understood as claims made in a royal record.

Language and script are different

The language of an inscription is the language in which its message is composed. The script is the system of written characters used to record that language. A question asking for the language is not asking for the script.

For example, the Ashokan inscriptions at Girnar use the Prakrit language written in Brahmi script. Rudradaman's inscription on the same rock uses Sanskrit written in Brahmi script. Thus, 2 inscriptions can use the same script without using the same language.

Most Ashokan inscriptions were written in Prakrit using Brahmi. There were regional exceptions elsewhere in the Mauryan world, including inscriptions using Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic. These exceptions do not change the identification of the Girnar edicts as Prakrit inscriptions in Brahmi script.

The 3 important inscription sites

This lesson concentrates on inscriptions associated with 3 locations:

  • Girnar or Junagadh, Gujarat: A rock bearing inscriptions associated with Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta.
  • Prayaga or Allahabad, Uttar Pradesh: A pillar bearing the famous Sanskrit prashasti of Samudragupta.
  • Aihole, Karnataka: The Meguti Jain temple, which bears an inscription praising the Chalukya ruler Pulakeshin II.

Girnar and Junagadh refer to the same inscription site in this context. The rock is located near Junagadh at the foot of Mount Girnar. Questions may use either name.

Prelims focus

  • Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions.
  • An edict communicates a ruler's message or instruction.
  • A prashasti praises a ruler or patron.
  • Prakrit and Sanskrit are languages; Brahmi is a script.
  • Girnar and Junagadh identify the same important rock-inscription site in Gujarat.
  • Trap: The use of Brahmi script does not mean that every inscription is in Prakrit.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Ch. 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed pp. 28–32 and 36–38; NCERT, Our Pasts – I, Class 6, Ch. 8, 'Ashoka, the Emperor Who Gave Up War', printed pp. 75–81; Shubhra Pramanik, 'Significant Discoveries around Sudarshan Lake, Junagadh', Puratattva, Vol. 35 (2004–05), p. 179.]

title: Understanding Inscriptions: Rulers, Languages, Scripts and Historical Records

body:
The Girnar rock and the Mauryan Empire

At the foot of Mount Girnar near Junagadh in Gujarat stands a large rock bearing important inscriptions from different periods of Indian history. The earliest inscriptions on this rock belong to Ashoka, the Mauryan emperor of the 3rd century BCE.

Ashoka issued messages on rocks and pillars across different regions of his empire. The Girnar site preserves a version of his 14 Major Rock Edicts. These are royal proclamations concerning the emperor's understanding of proper conduct, government and the welfare of his subjects.

Language and script

The Girnar edicts of Ashoka are written in the Prakrit language using the Brahmi script. They should not be described as Sanskrit inscriptions merely because later rulers added Sanskrit records to the same rock.

Prakrit was used in many early inscriptions because it could communicate a message in a language related to the speech of ordinary people. Brahmi supplied the written characters in which that message was engraved.

What do the edicts record?

The central subject of Ashoka's edicts is dhamma, a set of principles for ethical conduct and harmonious social life. Ashoka encouraged respect for parents and elders, kindness towards servants, compassion for living beings and consideration for people following different religious traditions.

His inscriptions also explain the responsibilities of officials and the importance of the welfare of the population. Their purpose was not simply to announce military victories. They communicated how Ashoka expected people and administrators to behave.

The Kalinga War and Rock Edict XIII

Major Rock Edict XIII is particularly associated with Ashoka's account of the suffering caused by the conquest of Kalinga. Kalinga was in the region of present-day Odisha. The edict expresses the emperor's remorse over the human cost of the war and emphasises the importance of conquest through dhamma rather than continued warfare.

This is an important distinction from the later royal prashastis, which generally concentrate on the military achievements and greatness of their patrons.

What the Girnar edicts do not record

Ashoka's own rock edicts at Girnar are primarily concerned with dhamma and royal instructions. The history of the construction and repair of Sudarshana Lake is given in later inscriptions on the same rock, especially that of Rudradaman I. The later inscription refers to improvements made to the lake during Ashoka's reign; that is not the principal subject of Ashoka's edicts.

Why the Gujarat location matters

The presence of Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts at Girnar establishes a direct connection between the Mauryan period and the region of present-day Gujarat. The same physical rock later received inscriptions under a Shaka ruler and a Gupta ruler. It therefore preserves evidence from several successive periods in one place.

Prelims focus

  • Girnar or Junagadh is in Gujarat, near Mount Girnar.
  • The earliest inscriptions on the Girnar rock belong to Ashoka of the Mauryan dynasty.
  • Ashoka's Girnar edicts date to the 3rd century BCE.
  • Language: Prakrit. Script: Brahmi.
  • The 14 Major Rock Edicts include teachings concerning dhamma.
  • Trap: Major Rock Edict XIII concerns Kalinga and remorse; the later Sudarshana Lake repair record belongs to Rudradaman.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – I, Class 6, Ch. 8, 'Ashoka, the Emperor Who Gave Up War', printed pp. 75–81; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Ch. 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed pp. 31–33; Shubhra Pramanik, 'Significant Discoveries around Sudarshan Lake, Junagadh', Puratattva, Vol. 35 (2004–05), p. 179; Archaeological Survey of India, BharatSHRI, 'Major and Minor Rock Edicts of Asoka from Erragudi', consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Ashoka's Girnar Rock Edicts: Dhamma and the Mauryan Message

body:
A Shaka ruler's inscription in Gujarat

Several centuries after Ashoka, a ruler of the Western Kshatrapas, also known as the Shakas, added an important inscription to the Girnar rock near Junagadh. The ruler was Rudradaman I, who held the title Mahakshatrapa, meaning Great Satrap.

His inscription is dated to Saka year 72, corresponding to approximately 150 CE. It is composed in Sanskrit prose and engraved in the Brahmi script. It is among the earliest substantial royal inscriptions in polished Sanskrit and is an important example of a royal prashasti.

Although the inscription praises Rudradaman's qualities and achievements, its most important contribution to this topic is its account of the Sudarshana Lake and the restoration of the reservoir's damaged embankment.

How Sudarshana Lake developed

Sudarshana Lake was an artificial reservoir near Girnar. It stored water through an embankment and was connected with water channels. The inscription describes its history across different reigns.

Construction under Chandragupta Maurya

The reservoir was originally constructed during the reign of Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Mauryan Empire. The work was undertaken by Pushyagupta, a provincial governor serving Chandragupta Maurya.

Improvement under Ashoka

During the reign of Ashoka, another provincial administrator named Tushaspha, described as a Yavana, made improvements by adding water channels. Thus, the original construction and the subsequent improvement both belong to the Mauryan period, but they are associated with different rulers and officials.

Restoration under Rudradaman I

Much later, during Rudradaman's reign, excessive rainfall and a violent storm caused serious damage to the lake's embankment. The water escaped through the breach, and restoration became necessary.

The inscription credits Rudradaman with arranging the reconstruction through his official Suvishakha, who administered the region of Anarta and Saurashtra. Anarta and Saurashtra were regions associated with western India, including parts of present-day Gujarat.

Rudradaman's record claims that the work was financed from his treasury without burdening the people through additional oppressive taxes or forced labour. This is a claim made by the royal inscription itself.

One lake, several rulers and officials

The sequence is important because the lake should not be attributed entirely to the ruler whose inscription gives the fullest description of it.

The work associated with Pushyagupta was the original construction. Tushaspha's work was an improvement through water channels. Rudradaman's intervention was a repair after storm damage. Each action belongs to a different stage in the reservoir's history.

Separate the ruler from the official

  • Chandragupta Maurya was the ruler; Pushyagupta was the official associated with construction.
  • Ashoka was the ruler; Tushaspha was the official associated with improvements.
  • Rudradaman I was the ruler; Suvishakha was the official associated with restoration.

The inscription shows that the maintenance of a reservoir could remain important under successive dynasties. It also demonstrates how a royal record could combine praise of a ruler with information about a specific public work.

Prelims focus

  • Rudradaman I belonged to the Western Kshatrapa or Shaka ruling tradition.
  • The Junagadh inscription is dated Saka year 72, approximately 150 CE.
  • Language: Sanskrit prose. Script: Brahmi.
  • Pushyagupta built Sudarshana Lake under Chandragupta Maurya.
  • Tushaspha improved the lake's water channels under Ashoka.
  • Trap: Rudradaman restored the damaged reservoir; he did not originally construct it.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Ch. 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed p. 38, 'The Sudarshana lake in Gujarat'; Archaeological Survey of India, BharatSHRI, 'Brahmi Inscription of Mahakshatrapa Rudradaman from Junagadh', consulted 19 November 2026; UGC–INFLIBNET, e-PG Pathshala, Indian Epigraphy, Module 29, 'Junagadh Inscription of Rudradaman', section 2–5, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The repair of Sudarshana Lake followed damage caused by heavy rainfall and flooding.

title: Rudradaman I's Junagadh Inscription: The History of Sudarshana Lake

body:
The Gupta-period record at Girnar

The Girnar rock at Junagadh also carries an inscription associated with Skandagupta, a ruler of the Gupta dynasty. This inscription belongs to the 5th century CE, several centuries after Rudradaman's record.

It is written in Sanskrit using a Gupta-period form of Brahmi script. It praises Skandagupta and records another episode in the history of Sudarshana Lake.

The record includes dates in the Gupta era corresponding approximately to 455–458 CE. For basic chronological identification, it is sufficient to associate the inscription with the middle of the 5th century CE.

Another flood damaged the reservoir

After the repair undertaken during Rudradaman's reign, the lake remained important. During Skandagupta's reign, heavy rainfall again damaged its embankment. Water escaped, and the reservoir required further restoration.

Skandagupta's provincial governor in Saurashtra was Parnadatta. The work of restoring the damaged embankment was carried out under the supervision of Parnadatta's son, Chakrapalita.

The inscription also records the construction of a temple dedicated to Vishnu by Chakrapalita. The central historical connection for the present topic, however, is the repair of Sudarshana Lake during Skandagupta's rule.

How this inscription differs from Rudradaman's

Both Rudradaman's and Skandagupta's inscriptions are in Sanskrit. Both concern repairs to the same reservoir near Girnar. However, they belong to different ruling dynasties and different centuries.

  • Rudradaman I: A Western Kshatrapa or Shaka ruler of the 2nd century CE. His official Suvishakha was associated with repairing the flood-damaged reservoir.
  • Skandagupta: A Gupta ruler of the 5th century CE. His governor Parnadatta and Parnadatta's son Chakrapalita were associated with the later restoration.

The repeated repairs demonstrate why the Sudarshana Lake inscriptions are especially useful for studying Gujarat's ancient history: records from distinct political periods refer to the maintenance of the same water resource.

The 3 rulers associated with the famous Girnar rock inscriptions are Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta. The original construction of Sudarshana Lake, however, is attributed to Pushyagupta during Chandragupta Maurya's reign.

Prelims focus

  • Skandagupta belonged to the Gupta dynasty.
  • His Junagadh inscription dates to the middle of the 5th century CE.
  • Language: Sanskrit. Script: Gupta-period Brahmi.
  • The inscription records another flood and repair of Sudarshana Lake.
  • Parnadatta was Skandagupta's governor in Saurashtra; Chakrapalita supervised the repair.
  • Trap: Suvishakha belongs to Rudradaman's repair, while Chakrapalita belongs to Skandagupta's.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Ch. 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed p. 38, 'The Sudarshana lake in Gujarat'; GCERT, History, Standard 11, Ch. 9, 'India During the Gupta Period', printed p. 58; 'The History of the Sudarsana Lake', reproduced in the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts archival collection, p. 43; Shubhra Pramanik, 'Significant Discoveries around Sudarshan Lake, Junagadh', Puratattva, Vol. 35 (2004–05), p. 179.]

title: Skandagupta's Junagadh Inscription: A Second Restoration of the Lake
